entry: Rivalry between the [[British Empire|British]] and [[Russian Empire|Russian]] empires over influence in 19th-century Central Asia. The contest centered on [[Afghanistan]], Persia and [[Tibet]], where both powers used military intervention and diplomacy. Russia conquered Turkestan, while Britain expanded and set the borders of British India. The empires never fought a full-scale war directly against each other, but they did battle in the [[Crimean War]] from 1853 to 1856. By the early 20th century, a line of independent states from the Caspian Sea to the Eastern Himalayas had become protectorates and territories of the two empires. The Anglo-Russian Convention of August 1907 formally delineated control in Afghanistan, Persia and Tibet. The term was coined in 1840 by Captain Arthur Conolly and popularized by [[Rudyard Kipling]]'s novel *Kim* (1901).

Group of five large interconnected freshwater lakes spanning the [[Canada]]–[[United States]] border. The lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario, though hydrologically Michigan and Huron are a single body of water, joined at the Straits of Mackinac. They are the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth by total area and the second-largest by total volume, holding more than 20% of the world's surface fresh water by volume. Their total surface is 94,250 square miles (244,106 sq km). The lakes began forming around 14,000 years ago at the end of the [[Last Glacial Period]], as retreating ice sheets exposed basins that filled with meltwater. They drain to the [[Atlantic Ocean]] through the Saint Lawrence River, and the Great Lakes Waterway enables shipping among them. Shipping, trade and fishing have long depended on the lakes, and major cities on their shores include [[Chicago]], [[Detroit]] and [[Toronto]].

Industrialization campaign in [[China]], 1958–1962. Initiated by [[Mao Zedong]], chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, it aimed to transform China from an agrarian society into an industrialized one through people's communes. Its methods included mass mobilization, mandatory collectivization and forced labor. Peasants were mobilized to supply grain, cash crops and even steel for urban industry, and procurement quotas set with false reports from the countryside worsened the [[Great Chinese Famine|famine]] of 1959–1961. Estimates of excess deaths range from 15 to 55 million, and their accuracy is disputed. Economist Dwight Perkins argues that heavy investment produced little gain, calling the campaign an expensive disaster. At the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference in 1962, Mao ceded day-to-day leadership to moderates including Liu Shaoqi and [[Deng Xiaoping]]. Mao launched the [[Cultural Revolution]] in 1966 to remove opposition and reconsolidate his power.

9th-century, predominantly West Slavic state in [[Central Europe]]. Centered on the Morava River, it occupied the area of today's Moravia in the eastern [[Czech Republic]] and adjacent western [[Slovakia]], and it possibly included territory in several neighboring countries. Its borders cannot be exactly determined, but it reached its largest extent under Prince Svatopluk I, who ruled from 870 to 894. The realm saw the rise of the first Slavic literary culture, in Old Church Slavonic. Missionaries [[Cyril and Methodius]] arrived in 863, introducing the Glagolitic alphabet, the first alphabet devoted to a Slavic language, and Slavonic liturgy, which Pope Adrian II later approved. Separatism and internal conflicts after Svatopluk's death contributed to the state's fall. The [[Hungary|Hungarians]] overran it, and its collapse occurred between 902 and 907.

Conflict between Sweden and a coalition led by Russia, 1700–1721. The allies were Peter I of Russia ([[Peter the Great]]), Frederick IV of Denmark–Norway and Augustus II the Strong of Saxony, who opposed Sweden under [[Charles XII of Sweden|Charles XII]]. Sweden parried the Danes at Travendal (August 1700) and the Russians at Narva (November 1700). Russia recovered and founded [[Saint Petersburg]] in 1703 to secure access to the Baltic Sea. Charles XII's main army was destroyed at the Battle of Poltava in 1709, after which the coalition revived and Hanover and Prussia joined it. Charles XII was killed in the trenches before Fredriksten during a campaign against Norway. The Treaty of Nystad (1721) ended the war, with Sweden losing its Baltic provinces and Russia becoming the dominant power in the Baltic region. Sweden's absolute monarchy had ended with Charles XII's death, and its Age of Liberty began.

Paleoproterozoic rise in free [[Oxygen|oxygen]] in Earth's atmosphere and shallow seas. The event began about 2.46–2.426 billion years ago and ended around 2.06 billion years ago. It is attributed to [[Cyanobacteria]], which evolved chlorophyll-based photosynthesis that released oxygen as a byproduct. The atmosphere changed from a weakly reducing state, practically devoid of oxygen, to an oxidizing one containing persistent free oxygen. Oxygen levels stayed below 1% to as high as about 10% of the present atmospheric level (PAL) for most of the Proterozoic. Free oxygen can oxidize organic compounds, and the event may have caused the extinction of many early, mostly anaerobic organisms. Symbiosis between surviving [[Archaea|archaea]] and aerobic proteobacteria, which became [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]], may have led to the rise of eukaryotic life.

Broad expanse of flatland in North America, east of the [[Rocky Mountains]]. It is the western part of the Interior Plains and is largely covered by [[Prairie|prairie]], [[Steppe|steppe]] and grassland. It covers most or all of Kansas, Nebraska, and North and South Dakota, eastern parts of Colorado, Montana and Wyoming, and the southern parts of [[Alberta]], [[Saskatchewan]] and [[Manitoba]]. Much of the region was once home to [[American bison]] herds, which were hunted to near extinction in the mid- to late 19th century. Nevin Fenneman's 1916 study *Physiographic Subdivision of the United States* brought the term "Great Plains" into wider use; before then the area was usually called the High Plains. Since European settlement, much of the native grassland has been converted to cropland and rangeland, making the area central to North American agriculture. In Canada the term is rarely used, and the region is known as the Canadian Prairies.

Political purge in the Soviet Union, 1936–1939. Launched by [[Joseph Stalin]] after the 1934 assassination of Sergei Kirov, it used show trials and mass operations to remove suspected dissenters from the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]], particularly [[Bolsheviks|Old Bolsheviks]]. The secret police, the NKVD, carried out most of the purge. Figures such as [[Nikolai Bukharin]] were removed, imprisoned or executed, and the purge reached the Red Army high command. Hundreds of thousands were accused of political crimes and were executed or sent to the [[Gulag]] labor camps. The purge peaked from September 1936 to August 1938 under NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov, hence the name *Yezhovshchina*. Scholars estimate the death toll at 700,000 to 1.2 million. In 1938 Stalin criticized the NKVD for mass executions and oversaw the executions of its chiefs, Genrikh Yagoda and Yezhov. [[Leon Trotsky]], who had been exiled, survived the purge but was later assassinated in Mexico on Stalin's orders.

Largest of the Egyptian pyramids, on the Giza Plateau near [[Cairo]], Egypt. It was built as the tomb of [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]] Khufu of the Fourth Dynasty, c. 2600 BC, over about 26 years. Hemiunu, Khufu's vizier, is believed by some to have been its architect. Initially 146.6 m (481 ft) tall, it was the world's tallest human-made structure for more than 3,700 years. Most of its smooth white limestone casing has since been removed, lowering it to 138.5 m (454.4 ft). The pyramid used an estimated 2.3 million large blocks weighing 6 million tonnes in total. Granite blocks weighing up to 80 tonnes were shipped by boat on the [[Nile]] from [[Aswan]] for the King's Chamber. It is the oldest of the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]] and the only one that remains largely intact. It forms part of the UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]] Memphis and its Necropolis.

International economic contraction from late 2007 to mid-2009. It overlapped the [[2008 financial crisis]] and began with the bursting of the United States housing bubble. The International Monetary Fund concluded that it was the most severe economic and financial meltdown since the [[Great Depression]]. In the U.S., the recession lasted from December 2007 to June 2009, while economies in [[China]], [[India]] and Indonesia continued to grow substantially.

Persistent high-pressure storm in the atmosphere of [[Jupiter]]. It is the largest anticyclonic storm in the [[Solar System]] and is located 22 degrees south of Jupiter's [[Equator|equator]]. Its red-orange color is attributed to a sunburn effect, in which high-altitude chemical compounds are broken down by solar radiation. Winds in the storm reach 496 km/h (308 mph). It was first observed in September 1831, and continuous observations began in 1878.

Debunked white nationalist conspiracy theory about race and culture. Coined by French author Renaud Camus in his 2011 book *Le Grand Remplacement*, it claims that white European populations are being deliberately replaced by non-white people, especially from Muslim-majority countries, through mass migration and falling birth rates, with the complicity of elites. Academic scholars have dismissed it as rooted in a misunderstanding of demographic statistics. Perpetrators of the 2019 [[Christchurch mosque shootings]] and the 2022 Buffalo shooting referred to the theory.

Series of contiguous depressions, about 6,500 km long, running from northern [[Syria]] to [[Mozambique]]. In its original definition the valley runs through the [[Red Sea]]. British geologist John Walter Gregory introduced the term in 1896, following work by Austrian geologist Eduard Suess. Geologists now prefer the Afro-Arabian Rift System, but the term remains in use in geography, zoology, ecology and paleontology. The northern section includes the [[Dead Sea]] transform boundary. The East African Rift splits south of the Afar triangle into the Albertine and Gregory rifts. Rift lakes include [[Lake Tanganyika]], which at 673 km is the longest freshwater lake in the world. Fossils and early stone tools from Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania date back 2.6 million years. Volcanism has built peaks such as [[Mount Kilimanjaro]], an inactive stratovolcano standing 5,895 m high.

Second-largest lake in the [[Northwest Territories]], Canada, after [[Great Bear Lake]], and the deepest in North America at 614 m (2,014 ft). It covers 27,200 sq km (10,500 sq mi) and is 469 km (291 mi) long. The [[Mackenzie River]] drains it, and its chief tributaries are the Hay, Slave, Lockhart and Taltson rivers. The name refers to the Slavey, a Dene people whom the Cree called "slaves". Gold discovered on its North Arm in the 1930s led to the founding of Yellowknife, now the territorial capital. On January 24, 1978, the Soviet satellite Kosmos 954, which carried a nuclear reactor, disintegrated, and pieces of its core fell near the lake.

United States national park straddling the [[Tennessee]]–[[North Carolina]] border. It protects much of the Great Smoky Mountains, a subrange of the [[Blue Ridge Mountains]] in the larger [[Appalachian Mountains]]. Its highest peak, Kuwohi, rises to 6,643 ft (2,025 m) and is the highest mountain in Tennessee. The park covers 522,419 acres (2,114.15 sq km) and is known for its waterfalls, biodiversity and historic structures from early settler communities. Congress chartered it in 1934, and [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] dedicated it in 1940. Its land and other costs were paid in part with federal funds, the first national park to be funded this way, and it became a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1983. With over 11 million visitors in 2025, it is the most visited national park in the United States. Tourism to the park contributes an estimated $2.5 billion annually to the local economy.

Limestone statue of a resting sphinx on the Giza Plateau, Egypt. The mythical creature has the head of a human and the body of a [[Lion|lion]]. The Sphinx was carved from the limestone bedrock of the plateau, and it faces east on the west bank of the [[Nile]]. Archaeological evidence suggests it was created during the reign of Khufu (c. 2590–2566 BC) or Khafre (c. 2558–2532 BC), and scholars disagree on whether its face represents Khufu or one of his sons. It measures 73 m (240 ft) long and 20 m (66 ft) high. Its nose was lost in what examinations suggest was a deliberate act with rods or chisels, though the circumstances are unknown. Contrary to a popular myth, cannon fire from [[Napoleon]]'s troops did not destroy it. The Sphinx is the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Supreme life force in the traditional beliefs of many Indigenous cultures in [[Canada]] and the [[United States]]. Interpretations vary, but the Great Spirit is generally conceptualized as an omnipresent supreme being or [[Deity|god]]. Among the Lakota it is *Wakan Tanka*, which describes everything as *wakan*, or holy; activist Russell Means preferred the translation "Great Mystery". Lakota prayers often begin with *Tunkasila*, meaning "grandfather, Great Spirit". In the [[Haudenosaunee]] tradition it is "the Creator", and among Algonquian peoples it is *Gitche Manitou*. Algonquian belief in *Manitou* holds that this force is omnipresent, manifesting in all things. Because of perceived similarities to the Christian deity, European missionaries drew comparisons between the two as a conversion technique.

Series of conflicts between the [[Ottoman Empire]] and the Holy League, 1683–1699. The league consisted of the [[Holy Roman Empire]], [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth|Poland-Lithuania]], [[Republic of Venice|Venice]], [[Tsardom of Russia|Russia]] and the Kingdom of Hungary. Fighting began in 1683, and the war ended with the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699. It was a resounding defeat for the Ottomans, who lost substantial territory in Hungary and Poland-Lithuania and part of the western [[Balkans]] for the first time. The war was also the first instance of Russia joining an alliance with Western Europe. France stayed out of the league, and [[Louis XIV]] instead besieged Philippsburg in 1688, triggering the separate Nine Years' War. After the Ottomans retook Belgrade in 1690, the war stalemated until the Holy League's victory at the Battle of Zenta in 1697.

Sparsely populated desert ecoregion in [[Western Australia]] and [[South Australia]]. It is [[Australia|Australia's]] largest desert, covering 348,750 sq km (134,650 sq mi) from the Eastern Goldfields of Western Australia to the Gawler Ranges. Explorer Ernest Giles was the first European to cross it, in 1875, and named it after [[Queen Victoria]]. The desert has sandhills, grassland plains, gibber plains and salt lakes. Average annual rainfall is 200 to 250 mm (7.9 to 9.8 in). Summer daytime temperatures range from 32 to 40 °C, and winter temperatures from 18 to 23 °C. Only the hardiest plants survive in much of the desert, including spinifex grasses and mulga shrubs. Wildlife includes [[Emu|emus]], red kangaroos and small marsupials, and 31% of the desert is in protected areas.

Series of fortifications along the historical northern borders of [[China]]. Built to protect against nomadic groups from the [[Eurasian Steppe]], the first walls date to the 7th century BC and were joined together in the [[Qin dynasty]]. Successive dynasties expanded the system, and the best-known sections were built by the [[Ming dynasty]] (1368–1644). The wall used watchtowers, troop barracks and signal fires, and it also controlled immigration and trade, including duties on goods carried along the [[Silk Road]]. It stretches 21,196.18 km (13,170.70 mi) from Liaodong in the east to Lop Lake in the west. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and was voted one of the New 7 Wonders of the World in 2007. By the 19th century, "the Great Wall of China" had become the standard English name.

Ruined medieval city in southeastern [[Zimbabwe]]. The city stands near Masvingo and served as the capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe from the 13th century. It was settled around 1000 AD, and major construction took place from the 11th to the 15th century before the city was abandoned in the 16th or 17th century. It is the largest stone structure in precolonial [[Southern Africa]], covering 7.22 sq km (2.79 sq mi). Its Great Enclosure has dry stone walls 11 m (36 ft) high, built without mortar, and it likely served as the royal residence. Earlier estimates put the peak population at around 20,000, but a study using archaeological, ethnographic and historical evidence suggests it did not exceed 10,000. European antiquarians looted the site between the 1890s and 1920s. Its African origin did not become scholarly consensus until the 1950s, and the modern independent state was named after the site.

Extinct flightless [[Auk|alcid]], *Pinguinus impennis*, of the North Atlantic. The bird was about 75 cm (29.5 in) tall, with a black back, a white belly and a heavy, hooked bill. Its wings were too short for flight, but it was a powerful swimmer. Demand for its down, and its use as food and fishing bait, largely eliminated European populations by the mid-16th century. The last two confirmed specimens were killed on Eldey, off Iceland, in 1844. It is not closely related to the [[Penguin|penguins]] of the Southern Hemisphere, which were named for their resemblance to it.

Large [[Shark|shark]] species, *Carcharodon carcharias*, of the mackerel shark family Lamnidae. It has a grayish upperside and a white underside. Adults commonly measure 4 to 5 m, and the largest reliably measured specimen was 6 m long. The species is an [[Apex predator|apex predator]] and is partially warm-blooded, an adaptation that allows it to remain active in colder waters. It has about 300 triangular, serrated teeth that are continuously replaced, and its fatty liver can exceed a quarter of its body weight, providing buoyancy. It preys on seals, dolphins, squid, fish and other sharks, and it is occasionally preyed on by [[Orca|orcas]]. The 1974 novel *Jaws* and its 1975 film adaptation portray it as a ferocious man-eater, but white sharks normally do not prey on humans, and most bites are due to curiosity or possibly mistaken identity. The IUCN lists the species as vulnerable worldwide and critically endangered in European and Mediterranean waters, and several governments have banned catching and killing it.

Grouping of larger islands in the [[Caribbean Sea]], including Cuba, [[Hispaniola]], [[Puerto Rico]] and Jamaica, together with Navassa Island and the [[Cayman Islands]]. Hispaniola is shared by Haiti and the [[Dominican Republic]]. Together with the [[Lesser Antilles]], the Greater Antilles make up the Antilles, which with the Lucayan Archipelago form the West Indies. Most of the islands are independent countries, while Puerto Rico and Navassa Island are unincorporated territories of the United States and the Cayman Islands are a British Overseas Territory. Spanish settlement followed Christopher Columbus's first voyage. The [[Haitian Revolution]] established Haiti as an independent nation from France in 1804, the first and only successful anti-slavery and anti-colonial insurrection by self-liberated slaves. Spain transferred Cuba and Puerto Rico to the United States after the Spanish–American War in 1898.

Administrative area in [[England]], coterminous with the [[London]] region. It contains 33 local government districts: the 32 London boroughs and the [[City of London]]. Created in 1965, it has a land area of 1,572 sq km (607 sq mi) and an estimated population of 9,122,909 in 2025. The [[River Thames]] is its defining geographic feature. The Greater London Authority, formed in 2000, is responsible for strategic government across the region, while the boroughs handle regular local government.
